prompt: In the shop's account `describe-availability-zones` maps `us-east-1a` to `use1-az6`. A partner's account must put its cache in the same physical zone. What should the partner do?

choices.text: Use `us-east-1a` too, since a zone name is fixed by the region
choices.why: In an older region AWS maps names to zones per account, so the partner's `us-east-1a` may be another building.

choices.text: Run the same command in its own account and use the name whose id is `use1-az6`
choices.why: Right. The id names the same zone in every account; each account translates it to its own name.

choices.text: Pick the zone with the lowest latency, measured from the shop
choices.why: Zones of one region are all a millisecond or two apart; latency does not identify one.

choices.text: Ask AWS support to align the two accounts' zone names
choices.why: Nothing needs aligning: the zone id already is the shared name, and the command prints it.

prompt: Every month 100 GB go from `sa-east-1` to `us-east-1`, and 100 GB come back from `us-east-1` to `sa-east-1`. At the prices of the list of 16 September 2026, what does the month's transfer between the regions cost, in dollars?
hint: Lesson 1. Each direction has its own price, paid by the region the bytes leave.

prompt: Match each place to what it is.

pairs.right: a separate failure inside a region
a region extended into a city that has none
AWS equipment inside a mobile operator's network
AWS racks in your own datacentre

right_distractors: a copy of AWS with accounts of its own

prompt: A build machine talks to its cache all day. If either one is lost, the build simply runs again later. Where should the cache go?

choices.text: In another zone, so a zone's failure leaves one of the two standing
choices.why: That is the right call for a database and its standby. Here the failure does not matter, and every byte across zones is paid on both sides.

choices.text: In another region, where the copy is safest
choices.why: Leaving São Paulo costs 0.138 per GB; a chatty pair across regions pays that on every exchange.

choices.text: In the same zone as the build machine
choices.why: Right. Within one zone, over private addresses, transfer is free, and losing both together costs only a rerun.

choices.text: Wherever is cheapest per hour; transfer inside a region is free
choices.why: Only inside one zone is it free. Between two zones of the region it is 0.01 per GB each way.

prompt: A policy names `arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:218935875641:orders`. A colleague says it is a queue in `shop-prod`, in São Paulo. What does the ARN itself say?

choices.text: Both are right: the region field is only where the queue was first created
choices.why: A queue does not move between regions; the fourth field is where it lives.

choices.text: Whatever the account, the queue is in Virginia
choices.why: Right. The fourth field is the region, `us-east-1`; the fifth is the account.

choices.text: Nothing about the account, since an SQS ARN leaves that field empty
choices.why: That is a bucket's ARN, which has no account and no region. This one carries both.

choices.text: That it is a queue in a separate partition, `us-east-1`
choices.why: The partition is the second field, `aws` here. `us-east-1` is a region of it.

prompt: `shop-staging` tries to create the bucket `shop-backups` and hears `BucketAlreadyExists`. No account of the shop's organisation has a bucket by that name. What can be concluded?

choices.text: Some account somewhere in AWS owns it, and AWS will not say which
choices.why: Right. Bucket names share one namespace across all of AWS, and the refusal names no owner on purpose.

choices.text: The management account owns it, since its buckets are hidden from members
choices.why: If the shop owned it, an account of the shop would show it. And from the owning account itself the answer would be `BucketAlreadyOwnedByYou`.

choices.text: The name was deleted recently and is waiting to be released
choices.why: The lesson gives no such cause; the code says the name is taken, by another account.

choices.text: `shop-staging` lacks the permission to create buckets
choices.why: A missing permission is `AccessDenied`. This code is about the name.

prompt: Service Quotas raised the VPC quota of `shop-staging` in `sa-east-1` to 10. What is the quota of `shop-staging` in `us-east-1`, and of `shop-prod` in `sa-east-1`?

choices.text: 10 and 10, because a raise applies to the whole organisation
choices.why: A quota is counted per account, so the organisation has no single number to raise.

choices.text: 10 and 5: the raise follows the account into every region
choices.why: The VPC quota is not global; it is counted in each region separately.

choices.text: 5 and 10, since the raise lands on the account that runs production
choices.why: A request raises the quota of the account that asked, never of another one.

choices.text: 5 and 5
choices.why: Right. A raise is for one quota in one region of one account; everywhere else stays at the default of five.

prompt: The shop adds an account `shop-dev` and, to save a mailbox, gives it `aws+shop-staging@example.com`, the address `shop-staging` already uses. What happens in AWS?

choices.text: The two accounts share one root user
choices.why: Each account has exactly one root user of its own; AWS does not let two accounts share an address to begin with.

choices.text: The creation fails with `EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS`
choices.why: Right. The root user's address is unique across AWS. moto let it through, so that refusal was not run.

choices.text: It works; only the account alias has to be unique
choices.why: The alias is unique too, but so is the address. That is what moto shows and AWS refuses.

choices.text: `shop-staging` loses its address, which moves to the newer account
choices.why: Nothing moves: the second account is simply not created.

prompt: `shop-prod`, `shop-staging` and `sandbox` each send 4,096 GB from `sa-east-1` to the internet in one month: 0.15 dollars per GB for the first 10,240 GB, then 0.138. All three are in one organisation. What is the month's total, in dollars, leaving out the free allowance?
hint: Lesson 3. The tiers count the organisation's usage added up.

prompt: An account with years of history joined the shop's organisation by invitation. From the management account, `assume-role` on `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` in it fails. What is the likeliest reason?

choices.text: The handshake has not been accepted, so the account is still outside the organisation
choices.why: Then it would not be a member at all. The account joined; what it lacks is something the organisation never made for it.

choices.text: The role exists, but its `AdministratorAccess` is removed when an account is invited
choices.why: Nothing is removed on joining. The role is simply not there to begin with.

choices.text: The role does not exist: only accounts the organisation created get it
choices.why: Right. An administrator of the invited account has to create it by hand, with the same trust policy and `AdministratorAccess`.

choices.text: Invited accounts may only be reached through their root user
choices.why: A role works in an invited account like in any other, once somebody creates it.

prompt: To tell which members came with a history of their own, read `describe-account`: an account that accepted an invitation reports its `JoinedMethod` as ___.
The security team wants GuardDuty run for the whole organisation, and the management account to stay out of daily work. What does Organizations offer for that?

choices.text: An OU for security, which runs the service for the accounts below it
choices.why: An OU holds accounts and rules; it runs nothing and has no resources of its own.

choices.text: Naming the `security` account as the service's delegated administrator
choices.why: Right. A member then does the organisation-wide job, and the management account keeps only the tree and the bill.

choices.text: Moving the management account into the `Security` OU
choices.why: Where it sits changes nothing about its powers, and the point was to keep work off it.

choices.text: A second organisation, owned by the `security` account
choices.why: An account belongs to one organisation at a time, so the tooling would see none of the shop's accounts.

prompt: A stolen administrator key of `shop-staging` is used for `iam:CreateUser` and for `ec2:RunInstances` in `us-east-1`. The shop's four guardrails are attached as lesson 4 left them. Which of the two calls get past the SCPs?

choices.text: Neither, since the region guardrail covers every action outside São Paulo
choices.why: `NotAction` exempts the global services, IAM among them, so the region deny does not touch `CreateUser`.

choices.text: Both, because an administrator key overrides the organisation's denies
choices.why: No identity in a member account can lift an SCP; that is what makes it a guardrail.

choices.text: `CreateUser` only
choices.why: Right. IAM is exempt from the region deny, and none of the four denies user creation; the machine in Virginia is refused.

choices.text: `RunInstances` only, because `protect-deployer` denies IAM writes
choices.why: That guardrail covers the `deployer` role alone, and the region deny refuses the machine.

prompt: A team creates a role called `deployer` in the `sandbox` account. Is it covered by `protect-deployer`?

choices.text: No: the policy is attached to `Workloads`, and `sandbox` is not below it
choices.why: Right. An SCP filters the accounts on its branch; the `*` in the ARN only lets one policy work in every account of that branch.

choices.text: Yes: the `*` in the account field of the ARN reaches every account
choices.why: The ARN says which roles a statement matches. Which accounts it applies to is decided by where the policy is attached.

choices.text: Yes, because SCPs on the root are copied into every account
choices.why: SCPs are never copied, and this one is on `Workloads`, not on the root.

choices.text: Only once the sandbox's allow list names IAM
choices.why: The allow list already includes `iam:*`, and an allow list protects nothing anyway: it only limits.

prompt: The shop's root carries `FullAWSAccess` and three guardrails. How many more SCPs can be attached directly to the root in AWS?
hint: Lesson 4. moto did not enforce the limit per target.

prompt: The developers need SQS in the sandbox, which the allow list on the `Sandbox` OU leaves out. Which change lets them use it?

choices.text: Attach an SCP allowing `sqs:*` to the `sandbox` account itself
choices.why: The account already allows everything. The OU above it still has no allow for SQS, and every level has to have one.

choices.text: Give the developers an IAM policy allowing `sqs:*`
choices.why: They need that too, but IAM cannot reach past the ceiling the OU sets.

choices.text: Add `sqs:*` to `sandbox-allow-list`, the policy on the OU
choices.why: Right. The levels intersect, so the allow has to be present at the OU, where it is missing.

choices.text: Attach `FullAWSAccess` to the root again
choices.why: The root has it already. The OU is the level that leaves SQS out.

prompt: In a month, an account records 10,000 configuration items and its Config rules make 150,000 evaluations. At the São Paulo prices of 11 September 2026 (0.003 per item; evaluations 0.001 for the first 100,000, then 0.0008), what does Config cost that month, in dollars?
hint: Lesson 5. Two lines on the bill, the second in two tiers.

prompt: A control refused a CloudFormation stack that would have made a public bucket. An hour later an engineer made the same bucket with `aws s3api`, and nothing refused it. Which kind of control was it?

choices.text: Preventive
choices.why: A preventive control is an SCP and judges every request, from the command line too.

choices.text: Detective
choices.why: A detective control refuses nothing: it reports a resource after it exists.

choices.text: Proactive
choices.why: Right. A CloudFormation hook only sees what goes through CloudFormation, which is exactly the gap the engineer walked through.

choices.text: Mandatory
choices.why: Mandatory is a level of guidance, not a kind of control, and the mandatory ones protect the landing zone itself.

prompt: The shop runs a landing zone under Control Tower. Which of these appear on its bill? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Config's configuration items, in every governed account
choices.why: Right: 0.003 dollars each in São Paulo, and the busiest account records most.

choices.text: Control Tower itself, per account governed
choices.why: Control Tower is free; what it switches on is charged.

choices.text: Config rule evaluations made by detective controls
choices.why: Right: each rule judging each resource is an evaluation, 0.001 for the first 100,000 of the month.

choices.text: The management events of the organisation trail
choices.why: The first copy of management events costs nothing, and the organisation trail is that copy.

choices.text: Storing the records in `log-archive`
choices.why: Right: the records sit in S3 there, and storage is charged like any other.

prompt: A payments workload arrives with a regulator's rules that no other part of the shop needs. Which controls fit it, and how are they switched on?

choices.text: Strongly recommended ones, on the root, so every account gets them
choices.why: Those are AWS's advice for any company; a regulator's needs belong to one part of the tree.

choices.text: Mandatory ones, which Control Tower adds when it sees the workload
choices.why: Mandatory controls are on from the start and protect the landing zone itself; they are not chosen per workload.

choices.text: None; Control Tower's controls cannot be chosen, only accepted
choices.why: Only the mandatory ones are fixed. The other two levels are a choice.

choices.text: Elective ones, switched on for the OU that holds it
choices.why: Right. Elective controls are for particular needs and are turned on OU by OU.

prompt: The shop's workflow on `main` of `shop/web` deploys through `deployer` with OIDC. Now a workflow on the `release` branch of the same repository must deploy too, and nothing else may. What changes?

choices.text: Drop the `sub` condition, since `aud` already limits the token to AWS
choices.why: Every workflow on GitHub gets tokens for the same audience; without `sub` the role trusts all of them, strangers included.

choices.text: Let the `sub` condition accept `repo:shop/web:ref:refs/heads/release` as well
choices.why: Right. `sub` names repository and branch; a second value for the same key is an alternative, and everything else stays refused.

choices.text: Create an IAM user with an access key for the release workflow
choices.why: That puts a long-term secret into GitHub, the very thing OIDC exists to avoid.

choices.text: Register a second OIDC provider for the `release` branch
choices.why: The issuer is the same for every branch, and IAM is told to trust it once per account.

prompt: A key id beginning `ASIA` turns up in a build log that was made public this morning. What is it, and how long is it worth?

choices.text: A user's long-term key, valid until somebody deletes it
choices.why: That prefix is `AKIA`. A user's key would indeed have to be found and deleted.

choices.text: A role's own permanent key, valid until the role is deleted
choices.why: A role has no key of its own; `create-access-key` for one answered `NoSuchEntity`.

choices.text: A session's temporary key, useless once the session expires
choices.why: Right. It works only with its secret and token, and the three are refused together at the expiry, an hour by default.

choices.text: A root user's key, valid for as long as the account exists
choices.why: A root user's key would be a long-term key too, with the `AKIA` prefix.

prompt: To tidy IAM, someone proposes a group `staff` that contains the groups `developers`, `data` and `finance`, so a policy on `staff` reaches everybody. What happens?

choices.text: It works, up to the ten groups a user may belong to
choices.why: Ten is how many groups one user may be in. It says nothing about groups inside groups.

choices.text: It cannot be built: a group holds users, never another group
choices.why: Right. The way to reach everybody is to put each user in `staff` too, or attach the policy to all three groups.

choices.text: It works, and `staff` can then be named as a role's principal
choices.why: A group is not a principal either way; AWS refuses a trust policy naming one.

choices.text: It works only if `staff` is given a password of its own
choices.why: A group has no password, no key and no way to sign anything.

prompt: Which of these jobs has to be done by the root user, by AWS's documentation?

choices.text: Creating the account's first IAM user
choices.why: Root can do it, but so can any principal allowed `iam:CreateUser`; it is not on the short list.

choices.text: Attaching a service control policy to the account
choices.why: SCPs are attached from the management account's Organizations, and they limit the member's root.

choices.text: Changing or cancelling the support plan
choices.why: Right. With changing the account's name, e-mail or root password and closing the account, it is one of the few tasks that need root.

choices.text: Turning on MFA for bia's user
choices.why: Any administrator may do that; nothing about bia's factor needs root.

prompt: A statement allows `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::shop-assets/home/${aws:username}/*`, and the policy has no `Version` line. What does bia get?

choices.text: Her own prefix, `home/bia/`, since the variable is replaced by her name
choices.why: That happens under `2012-10-17`. A document with no `Version` is read as the old language.

choices.text: Only a prefix literally named `${aws:username}`, which nobody uses
choices.why: Right. With no `Version` the document is `2008-10-17`, where policy variables are plain text.

choices.text: Every prefix of the bucket, since an unknown variable matches anything
choices.why: An unread variable is not a wildcard; it is the characters as written.

choices.text: A refusal of the document, since `Version` is required
choices.why: The document is accepted and read as the old version, which is why the line is worth writing every time.

prompt: A policy document is 3,000 characters long. Where does AWS let it go, by the limits lessons 4 and 7 gave? Choose all that apply.
hint: Lesson 7, and lesson 4 for the organisation's policies.

choices.text: A customer-managed policy attached to bia
choices.why: Right: a managed policy may hold 6,144 characters.

choices.text: An inline policy on bia's user
choices.why: A user's inline policies hold only 2,048 characters, which is a hint about what they are for.

choices.text: An inline policy on the group `developers`
choices.why: Right: a group's inline policies may hold 5,120.

choices.text: A service control policy attached to `shop-prod`
choices.why: Right: lesson 4 gave an SCP's limit as 5,120 characters. It would fit, though it would grant nothing.

prompt: Put in order the start of a lesson that needs moto to judge permissions, from a stopped moto to the first command run as `admin`.
items: start `INITIAL_NO_AUTH_ACTION_COUNT=3 moto_server -p 4567`
create the user `admin`
attach `AdministratorAccess` to `admin`
create an access key for `admin` and keep it in a variable
`export` the key's id and secret
run `aws sts get-caller-identity`
trap: The key has to be the third request: a fourth signed with `test` is refused, and there is no way back but a restart.

prompt: A statement allows `s3:*Object` on `arn:aws:s3:::shop-assets/*`. Which of these actions does it NOT cover?

choices.text: `s3:DeleteObject`
choices.why: `*` matches any run of characters, so `Delete` before `Object` is covered.

choices.text: `s3:ListBucket`
choices.why: Right. Its name does not end in `Object`, and it acts on the bucket, which `shop-assets/*` does not name either.

choices.text: `s3:PutObject`
choices.why: `Put` is a run of characters before `Object`, so it matches.

choices.text: `s3:GetObject`
choices.why: Matched like the others, and it acts on objects, which is what the resource names.

prompt: In one account, the bucket policy of `shop-assets` allows `s3:GetObject` to `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/caio`. caio's own policies say nothing about S3. In AWS, can he read an object?

choices.text: Yes: within one account, one granting layer is enough
choices.why: Right. The bucket policy is a granting layer and nothing denies. Both sides must grant only across accounts.

choices.text: No: his identity policy must allow it as well
choices.why: That is the rule across accounts. Here caller and bucket share an account.

choices.text: No: a bucket policy can only deny, never grant
choices.why: A resource-based policy is a granting layer, like an identity policy.

choices.text: Only with MFA, which a bucket policy always demands
choices.why: MFA is a condition somebody writes; this policy has none.

prompt: ana must hand edu a session of `deployer` that can only read S3 for one afternoon, without making a second role. What does lesson 8 offer for that?

choices.text: A permission boundary on `deployer`
choices.why: A boundary limits every session of the role, the pipeline's included, not one afternoon's.

choices.text: An SCP on the account for the afternoon
choices.why: An SCP limits everybody in the account, and is set by the organisation, not by whoever assumes a role.

choices.text: A session policy passed to `assume-role` with `--policy`
choices.why: Right. It narrows that one session; what it can do is what both the role and the session policy allow.

choices.text: An inline policy on edu allowing only S3 reads
choices.why: Inside the session edu's own policies play no part; the role's permissions apply.

prompt: A policy allows `s3:*` on every resource when `aws:ResourceTag/team` equals `${aws:PrincipalTag/team}`. bia is tagged `team=web`, and a bucket is tagged `team=data`. In AWS, can she delete objects in it?

choices.text: Yes, because `s3:*` covers the deletion
choices.why: The action matches, but the condition does not, and a statement whose condition fails allows nothing.

choices.text: Yes, but only after a session policy names the tag
choices.why: A session policy can only limit, never grant.

choices.text: No, because the policy explicitly denies other teams
choices.why: There is no `Deny` here. The refusal is the implicit deny of a request nothing allowed.

choices.text: No: `web` is not `data`, so nothing allows it
choices.why: Right. Each team gets its own things; the request falls back to where every request starts.

prompt: The shop wants a list of every bucket, queue and key in its organisation that an account outside the organisation can reach. Which tool gives it?

choices.text: `aws iam simulate-principal-policy`, run for each outsider
choices.why: The simulator answers for a principal you name. The point here is the outsiders nobody named.

choices.text: An IAM Access Analyzer created for the organisation
choices.why: Right. An analyzer lists every resource whose policy lets somebody outside its zone of trust in.

choices.text: `aws accessanalyzer validate-policy` on each SCP
choices.why: The validator checks a document's grammar before it is saved; it does not list what is shared.

choices.text: moto, with its checking on, asked from a second account
choices.why: moto does not judge resource-based policies, so it would let everything through.

prompt: A role in `shop-prod` trusts `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/platform-admin`, a role in the management account. caio, an administrator there, calls `assume-role` on it straight from his own user. What does AWS answer?

choices.text: A session, since his `AdministratorAccess` allows `sts:AssumeRole`
choices.why: His side allows it, but the trust policy is the other half, and it names a role, not him.

choices.text: A refusal: only sessions of `platform-admin` may come through
choices.why: Right. That is the tighter form of cross-account trust; caio first assumes `platform-admin`, if its own trust lets him.

choices.text: A session, because the trust policy names his account
choices.why: It names one role of that account. Naming `:root` would have opened it to the account.

choices.text: A refusal, because no role can trust another account's role
choices.why: Trusting one role in another account is allowed, and it is the narrower choice.

prompt: `deployer` trusts bia, and her own policy allows `sts:AssumeRole` on it. `deployer` has no permission policies at all. What can bia's session do?

choices.text: Whatever bia's own policies allow, since the role adds nothing
choices.why: A session does not keep the caller's permissions; bia's policy only got her in.

choices.text: Everything, because a role with no policies is unrestricted
choices.why: No policy is no allow, and every request starts denied.

choices.text: Almost nothing: `sts get-caller-identity` still answers it
choices.why: Right. The session has the role's permissions, which are none; `get-caller-identity` answers for anybody.

choices.text: Nothing: STS refuses a session for a role without policies
choices.why: STS judges the trust and the caller's side; both agree, so the session is issued.

prompt: A role's trust policy names `"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:root"`. In AWS, which of these may assume it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `admin` in `123456789012`, holding `AdministratorAccess`
choices.why: Right. The trust names his account, and his own policies allow `sts:AssumeRole`. moto refused this one, comparing ARNs as strings.

choices.text: A user in `123456789012` whose only policy allows `sts:AssumeRole` on that role
choices.why: Right. Trusting the account hands the decision to that account's identity policies, and this one allows it.

choices.text: A user in `123456789012` with no policies at all
choices.why: His side grants nothing, and both sides have to agree.

choices.text: An administrator of `444455556666`, another account
choices.why: His own policies allow it, but the trust policy names a different account.

prompt: A profile that names a role makes the command line assume it and keep the session until it expires, in the directory `~/.aws/cli/___`.
dani wants one budget that warns her when the web team's spending passes 300 dollars in a month, across all six accounts. Where is it made, and what must be true first?

choices.text: In management, filtered by an activated `team` tag
choices.why: Right. The management account sees every account's charges, and a tag filter only works on a key billing knows.

choices.text: In each of the six accounts, one budget of 50 dollars apiece
choices.why: Six budgets watch six totals, none of them the web team's; a team spending 290 in one account sets off nothing.

choices.text: In `shop-prod`, since that is where most of the web team's cost is
choices.why: A budget in a member account watches that account alone, and staging's share would go unseen.

choices.text: In any account, as long as the web team's resources carry the tag
choices.why: The tag on the resource is one gate; activation in the management account is the other, and the budget has to see every account.

prompt: A brand-new account gets `shop-monthly` on its first day, with its two notifications. In the first weeks, which of them can fire?

choices.text: Only the forecasted one, which is the early warning
choices.why: It is the early warning, but it needs history to forecast from, and the account has none.

choices.text: Only the actual one, at 80%
choices.why: Right. AWS needs about five weeks of history before it forecasts anything, so the actual alert is the only one working at first.

choices.text: Both, from the first refresh of the day
choices.why: The actual one can; the forecast has nothing to project from yet.

choices.text: Neither, until the budget's first full month has ended
choices.why: An actual alert fires at the first refresh after 40 dollars have gone, whatever day that is.

prompt: A report grouped by `team` shows a large `team$` remainder, and nobody knows who started those resources. Which tag key could have said so without anybody writing it?

choices.text: `team`, once a tag policy fixes its values
choices.why: A tag policy fixes the spelling; it does not require the tag, so an untagged resource passes it.

choices.text: `project`, which every resource of the shop carries
choices.why: It is written by people too, and these resources carry none.

choices.text: `aws:createdBy`, an AWS-generated key, activated in Billing
choices.why: Right. AWS writes the identity that created the resource; like a user-defined key, it has to be activated to reach a report.

choices.text: `env`, backfilled for the last twelve months
choices.why: A backfill applies an activation to past months; it cannot add a tag a resource never had.

prompt: A new account lives on an AWS promotion. For its cost budget to show the usage rather than a bill near zero, the budget's `CostTypes` must set `Include___` to `false`.

A staging `m7i.large` in São Paulo runs 12 hours a day for 30 days. On demand is 0.16065 an hour; the one-year standard reservation, no upfront, is 72.68 a month whatever runs. How many dollars a month does staying on demand save?
hint: Lesson 14. Count the hours first, then compare with the break-even.

prompt: If `sa-east-1a` runs short of capacity, the shop's recovery plan must still be able to start an `m7i.large` there. Which purchase gives that, by lesson 14?

choices.text: A regional standard reservation for `m7i.large`
choices.why: A regional reservation is a discount in any zone of the region, and it sets no capacity aside anywhere.

choices.text: A zonal reservation in `sa-east-1a`
choices.why: Right. A zonal reservation applies only in its zone, and in exchange it also reserves the capacity there.

choices.text: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the `m7i` family
choices.why: A Savings Plan commits to dollars an hour and holds no machine for you.

choices.text: A Compute Savings Plan, which follows the workload anywhere
choices.why: It follows the usage on the bill; it does not make room in a zone.

prompt: Five months into a one-year commitment, the shop stops needing it. Which of its commitments could it sell to somebody else?

choices.text: A Compute Savings Plan
choices.why: AWS's documentation says no Savings Plan can be sold or exchanged once bought.

choices.text: A convertible Reserved Instance
choices.why: A convertible one can be exchanged for another convertible of equal or greater value, not sold.

choices.text: A standard Reserved Instance
choices.why: Right. A standard reservation can be sold on AWS's Reserved Instance Marketplace.

choices.text: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan
choices.why: Priced like a standard reservation, but a Savings Plan all the same: it cannot be sold.

prompt: `shop-prod` holds a standard reservation for an `m7i.large` and a Compute Savings Plan of 0.10915 an hour, and in one hour it runs a single `m7i.large`. Which commitment covers that instance?

choices.text: The Savings Plan, since its rate is the higher of the two
choices.why: The order is fixed and does not depend on the rate.

choices.text: Both, each paying half of the hour
choices.why: An hour of usage is covered once; nothing is split between commitments.

choices.text: The RI; the plan's hour goes to other usage, or is lost
choices.why: Right. Reservations are applied first, and Savings Plans to what is left, here in another account of the organisation if any.

choices.text: Whichever was bought first
choices.why: The purchase date plays no part; AWS documents the order by kind.

prompt: The shop's first data export is created in `shop-staging`, because that is where the cost questions are. What will its files cover?

choices.text: The whole organisation, since every account shares one bill
choices.why: The bill is the management account's; a member's export sees that member.

choices.text: `shop-staging` alone; an export for the organisation belongs in the management account
choices.why: Right. The consolidated bill belongs to the management account, for the same reason cost allocation tags are activated there.

choices.text: Nothing, because a member account cannot create an export
choices.why: The lesson places an export in the management account when it should cover the organisation, not because a member is refused.

choices.text: Every account, but with no tags
choices.why: Which accounts appear depends on where the export lives, and tags depend on activation, not on the account.

prompt: In October the instance under the Savings Plan ran only half the month, and `team.sql` was run unchanged. What does its amortised column get wrong?

choices.text: Nothing: amortised spreads the fee over the hours used
choices.why: It charges each covered line its effective cost; the hours with nothing to cover have no line to carry them.

choices.text: It charges the web team the whole month's fee
choices.why: It charges the web team only the covered half; the problem is where the other half went.

choices.text: The unused half of the commitment disappears from every row
choices.why: Right. The query sets the fee line to zero, so idle hours that were paid for land on nobody, and the total falls short of the bill.

choices.text: It counts the covered hours twice, as unblended does
choices.why: Unblended does not count them twice either: covered usage and its negation cancel.

prompt: In CUR 2.0, a tag that somebody wrote, such as `team`, appears inside `resource_tags` with the prefix `___`, which tells it apart from one AWS generated.
The shop's real report reaches millions of rows of Parquet, and `team.sql` moves from `sqlite3` to Amazon Athena. What has to change in it?

choices.text: The grouping, since Athena cannot `GROUP BY` a tag
choices.why: The `GROUP BY` stays as it is.

choices.text: Nothing at all: the SQL is the same everywhere
choices.why: Almost nothing, but `json_extract` is this file's stand-in for a map, and Athena reads a real one.

choices.text: The column names, which the real report spells differently
choices.why: `cur.csv` uses the real names, which is what makes the queries carry over.

choices.text: Only how the map of tags is read
choices.why: Right. Athena reads the `resource_tags` map with its own syntax instead of `json_extract`; the `GROUP BY` stays.

prompt: The shop has a public zone and a private zone, both named `shop.example.com`, the private one associated with the production VPC. A server in that VPC asks for `api.shop.example.com`. Which zone answers?

choices.text: The public one, because it was delegated at the registrar
choices.why: Delegation sends the internet's resolvers to the public zone; inside the VPC the Resolver asks the private zones first.

choices.text: The internal zone, which its network is linked to
choices.why: Right. That is split-horizon DNS: one name, an internal answer for the shop's machines and a public one for everybody else.

choices.text: Neither: two zones with one name are refused
choices.why: A public and a private zone may share a name; it is a documented arrangement.

choices.text: Whichever was created first
choices.why: The order of creation plays no part; the association does.

prompt: Match each need of the shop to the routing policy that meets it.

pairs.left: send one search request in ten to a new cluster
answer from the region with the lowest measured network delay
answer with a standby while the primary's health check fails
show a page only to viewers in Brazil, whatever the network

prompt: At three in the morning the search canary, weighted 10 beside 90, starts answering errors. What is the quickest way to stop sending it traffic and keep the record for later?

choices.text: Delete the canary's record with a `DELETE` batch
choices.why: That stops it, and the record is gone; the point was to keep it.

choices.text: Raise the current record's weight to 1000
choices.why: The canary would still get 10 answers in 1,010: a share, not zero.

choices.text: `UPSERT` the canary with a weight of 0
choices.why: Right. A weight of 0 takes a record out of rotation without deleting it; caches still hold the old answer for the TTL, 60 seconds here.

choices.text: Lower the canary's TTL to 1 second
choices.why: A TTL decides how long an answer is kept, not how often it is given.

prompt: The Virginia standby, `198.51.100.20`, gets a health check of its own, probing over HTTPS every 30 seconds. At the list of 11 September 2026, what does that check cost a month?

choices.text: Nothing: the first 50 health checks are free
choices.why: Only checks of AWS endpoints are free for the first 50, and this address is outside AWS.

choices.text: 0.75 dollars
choices.why: That is a check of a non-AWS address with no options. HTTPS counts as one.

choices.text: 2.75 dollars
choices.why: Right: 0.75 for a non-AWS endpoint, plus 2.00 because HTTPS is one of the optional features.

choices.text: 0.50 dollars
choices.why: That is a check of an AWS endpoint past the first 50.

prompt: A server in the shop's datacentre, reached over lesson 24's VPN, must sit behind the ALB beside the machines in the VPC. Which target group can hold it?

choices.text: An `instance` group, registering the server by its name
choices.why: `instance` registers machines by EC2 id, and a server in the datacentre has none.

choices.text: One of type `ip`, registering the server's address
choices.why: Right. `ip` targets are how a machine in a peered VPC or the datacentre gets behind an ALB; the type is chosen at creation and never changed.

choices.text: The existing `shop-web-app` group, after changing its type to `ip`
choices.why: A target group's type cannot be changed later; a new group is needed.

choices.text: A `lambda` group, with a function forwarding to the server
choices.why: A `lambda` target is a function that answers the request itself, not a relay.

prompt: To protect the staff pages, a colleague adds a rule: forward to the staff target group only when the header `X-Staff: yes` is present, and answer 403 otherwise. What has the rule achieved?

choices.text: Protection, because only an ALB can read the header
choices.why: Only an ALB reads it, but anybody can write it: the header is what the caller chose to send.

choices.text: Protection, as long as the listener is HTTPS
choices.why: TLS hides the header from people on the way, not from the caller who writes it.

choices.text: Nothing, since a fixed response cannot follow a forward rule
choices.why: Rules of both kinds sit side by side on one listener, as the shop's own do.

choices.text: Routing only: whoever sends that header gets in
choices.why: Right. A rule decides where a request goes, never who may make it; authentication, security groups or WAF decide that.

prompt: A teammate creates the HTTPS listener and leaves out `--ssl-policy`, trusting the default. What does the lab's answer warn about?

choices.text: Its default still accepts TLS 1.0 and 1.1
choices.why: Right. In the lab the default was `ELBSecurityPolicy-2016-08`; naming `ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06` accepts only 1.2 and 1.3, which every browser the customers use speaks.

choices.text: The listener is refused without a policy
choices.why: It is created, with a default; that is the problem.

choices.text: The default accepts only TLS 1.3, which old browsers lack
choices.why: It is the other way round: the default is the older, wider policy.

choices.text: The certificate is ignored until a policy is named
choices.why: The certificate and the policy are separate settings of the listener.

prompt: Put in order what happens to a customer's request for `https://shop.example.com/api/orders`, from the name to the machine that answers.
items: the name resolves to the address of one of the load balancer's nodes
that node accepts the connection on the listener for port 443
the listener tries its rules from the lowest priority up
the rule on `/api/*` picks the target group `shop-api`
a healthy target in that group answers
trap: The machines are attached to the target group, not to the load balancer: the group is chosen before any machine is.

prompt: In a month the shop sends 1,024 GB through CloudFront to viewers in the US, in 20 million HTTPS requests. At the list of 16 September 2026, what do transfer and requests cost together, in dollars?
hint: Lesson 23. The viewer's place sets the price, not the shop's region.

prompt: A release script runs `create-invalidation --paths "/*"` after every deployment, ten times a month. What does that cost the shop?

choices.text: Nothing at all: ten paths are well inside the free thousand
choices.why: The line on the bill is free indeed, but that is not the whole cost.

choices.text: Ten emptied caches, and almost nothing billed
choices.why: Right. A wildcard is one path, but `/*` sends every viewer's next request to the origin at once, after each release.

choices.text: 0.005 dollars for every file the wildcard matches
choices.why: AWS counts a wildcard path as one path, however many files it covers.

choices.text: Nothing, and the browsers fetch the new files at once
choices.why: An invalidation clears CloudFront's caches only; a browser keeps its copy for as long as its header said.

prompt: The API behaviour uses `CachingDisabled` with `AllViewer`, and the API now reads the viewer's `Accept-Language`. A colleague proposes adding that header to a cache key. What does the lesson say?

choices.text: It is needed, or the header never reaches the origin
choices.why: What reaches the origin is the origin request policy's business, and `AllViewer` forwards every header.

choices.text: Not needed: what reaches the origin is a separate setting, and it sends everything
choices.why: Right. Forwarding and keying are separate questions, and with caching disabled there is no key to divide anyway.

choices.text: It is needed, and it should go on `/static/*` too
choices.why: On `/static/*` it would make one copy of each image per language, dividing the hit rate for nothing.

choices.text: It is refused, since a managed policy cannot carry a header
choices.why: Managed policies carry headers; `AllViewer` forwards all of them.

prompt: The shop creates an AWS WAF web ACL in `sa-east-1`, with the regional scope, and cannot attach it to the distribution. What does CloudFront need instead?

choices.text: The same web ACL, attached to the bucket origin instead
choices.why: WAF filters at the edge for CloudFront; the bucket is closed by OAC, not by WAF.

choices.text: A web ACL in every region where it has edges
choices.why: A distribution is global and takes one web ACL, made in one place.

choices.text: Shield Advanced, which replaces WAF on a distribution
choices.why: Shield is about floods of traffic and does not replace WAF's rules.

choices.text: Another one, scoped `CLOUDFRONT`, made in `us-east-1`
choices.why: Right. Like its certificates, what CloudFront attaches comes from `us-east-1`, wherever the shop lives.

prompt: The shop's route table sends `192.168.0.0/16` to the virtual private gateway, with `CreateRoute` in its `Origin` column. The office adds `172.16.0.0/16` and announces it over BGP, and the VPC cannot reach it. Why?

choices.text: BGP cannot announce more than one network over a tunnel
choices.why: Announcing several prefixes is BGP's ordinary job.

choices.text: Propagation is off: the table holds only what was typed
choices.why: Right. With propagation on from the gateway, the table receives what the gateway learnt; its route would say `EnableVgwRoutePropagation`.

choices.text: The customer gateway must be created again with the new range
choices.why: A customer gateway records an address and an AS number, not the office's networks.
The two ranges share no address.

prompt: `VgwTelemetry` for the office's VPN shows one tunnel `UP` and the other `DOWN`, and the office still reaches the VPC. What should the shop do?

choices.text: Nothing: one tunnel up is the normal state
choices.why: Two tunnels up is the design; with one, the next maintenance on that tunnel's end takes the office off the VPC.

choices.text: Delete the VPN connection and create a single-tunnel one
choices.why: Every VPN connection is two tunnels; there is no single-tunnel kind to create.

choices.text: Bring the second tunnel up before AWS maintains the first one's end
choices.why: Right. AWS maintains its two ends one at a time; the office survives that only with both tunnels configured and up.

choices.text: Switch from BGP to static routes, which keep a tunnel up
choices.why: Static routes fail over worse, not better: the router has to notice a dead tunnel itself.

prompt: The shop has two Direct Connect connections, both at Equinix SP4, on separate AWS devices. Which failure does that arrangement NOT survive?

choices.text: One of AWS's devices failing
choices.why: Separate devices are exactly what this arrangement buys.

choices.text: A port failing on one connection
choices.why: The other connection carries on; that is the development-and-test model's purpose.

choices.text: The building going dark
choices.why: Right. Both connections are in one location; surviving a building takes one connection at each of two.

choices.text: A cross-connect being cut on one of the two
choices.why: Each connection has its own cross-connect, so the second still works.

prompt: Put these designs for the office's road in order of their monthly charge for hours alone, cheapest first, at the lists of 17 September 2026 and 730 hours.
items: a VPN to the virtual private gateway
a VPN ending on a Transit Gateway
one dedicated 1 Gbps port at Equinix SP4
one dedicated 1 Gbps port, with a VPN behind it
a dedicated 1 Gbps port at each of two locations
trap: A Transit Gateway attachment is charged on top of the VPN's own hour, 0.09 against 0.05, and it is still far below a port's 0.30.

prompt: The shop's web servers must read `shop-assets` and also send messages to a queue. A colleague makes two roles, `shop-app` and `shop-app-queue`, and wants both on the instance. What does the lesson say?

choices.text: Attach two instance profiles, one for each role
choices.why: An instance carries one profile association, and the profile is where the role goes.

choices.text: Use one role whose policies grant both
choices.why: Right. A profile holds exactly one role; moto refused the second with `LimitExceeded`, as AWS documents.

choices.text: Put both roles into the `shop-app` profile
choices.why: That is the call that failed: `InstanceSessionsPerInstanceProfile` is 1.

choices.text: Copy a key for the second role onto the disk
choices.why: A role has no key of its own, and a key on the disk is what profiles exist to avoid.

prompt: CloudTrail shows a bucket read by `arn:aws:sts::123456789012:assumed-role/shop-app/i-0ee42130b0c3e009d`. What does the last part tell you?

choices.text: The access key that signed the call
choices.why: A key id starts with `AKIA` or `ASIA`; this is a session name.

choices.text: The name of the instance profile
choices.why: The profile is `shop-app` too; the last part names something else.

choices.text: Which machine made the call: the session is named after the instance
choices.why: Right. On EC2 the role's session name is the instance id, so the log points at one machine.

choices.text: The person who launched the instance
choices.why: Who launched it is a separate `RunInstances` event; this call was the machine's own.

prompt: Some of the shop's EKS pods will run on Fargate, and each needs a role of its own. Which mechanism does the lesson point to for them?

choices.text: EKS Pod Identity, the simpler choice
choices.why: It is simpler on EKS, but its agent does not reach pods on Fargate.

choices.text: The node's instance profile, with a hop limit of 2
choices.why: That shares one role with every pod, which is what a role per workload avoids.

choices.text: An ECS task role
choices.why: Task roles belong to ECS tasks, not to pods on EKS.

choices.text: IRSA, a token traded at STS
choices.why: Right. IRSA stays where Pod Identity does not reach, such as pods on Fargate.

prompt: Match each way a workload gets a role to where its credentials are found.
A permission set is given `PT12H`, and the Identity Center session lasts the default eight hours. Nine hours after `aws sso login`, a command with that profile runs. What happens?

choices.text: It works: the role credentials last twelve hours
choices.why: The permission set bounds each set of role credentials; the sign-in has its own, shorter clock.

choices.text: It says the token has expired, and `aws sso login` is needed again
choices.why: Right. The Identity Center session limits the sign-in itself, and it ended at eight hours.

choices.text: It falls back to the test keys `env.sh` exports
choices.why: A profile named with `--profile` takes the environment's keys out of the chain.

choices.text: It works until the role credentials reach twelve hours, then stops
choices.why: New role credentials need the sign-in's token, and the token died at eight hours.

prompt: bia signs in to `shop-staging` with `Developer`, which is AWS's `PowerUserAccess`, and tries to create an IAM role for her test. What happens?

choices.text: It works: power users may do everything
choices.why: Everything except managing IAM and the organisation, which is exactly this.

choices.text: It works, but only in the accounts where she has `ReadOnly`
choices.why: `ReadOnly` changes nothing anywhere; it would not help either.

choices.text: It is refused: `PowerUserAccess` leaves out managing IAM
choices.why: Right. That is the usual line between building in an account and governing it.

choices.text: It is refused, because Identity Center users cannot call IAM
choices.why: They act as a role, and a permission set that allowed IAM would let them.

prompt: A team enables an account instance of Identity Center inside `shop-staging`, hoping to give its people access to `shop-staging` and `shop-prod`. What does the lesson say about that?

choices.text: It works, as long as SCIM is connected
choices.why: SCIM provisions users and groups; it does not change what an account instance can do.

choices.text: It cannot: that kind serves applications only
choices.why: Right. Access to accounts comes from the organisation instance, enabled once in the management account.

choices.text: It works for `shop-staging` only
choices.why: An account instance gives access to no AWS account, its own included.

choices.text: It replaces the organisation instance for that branch of the tree
choices.why: Instances do not follow the tree; the organisation has one instance for account access.

prompt: A server in the office can be given an X.509 certificate from a certificate authority the account trusts. Instead of an access key, it can assume a role through IAM Roles ___.
A copy of `erp-sync`'s current key turns up in a public paste. Its only policy is `upload-erp.json`. Before anybody acts, what can whoever found it do?

choices.text: Read every backup in `shop-backups`
choices.why: The policy allows `s3:PutObject` only; there is no `GetObject` in it.

choices.text: Create a new user with a key of its own
choices.why: That needs IAM permissions, and `erp-sync` has none.

choices.text: Put files under `erp/` in `shop-backups`, overwriting what is there
choices.why: Right. A key that has to exist should do as little as possible, and this one can only upload to one prefix.

choices.text: Nothing, since the key works only from the office
choices.why: An access key works from any network; nothing ties it to a place.

prompt: dani's leaked key is now `Inactive`. CloudTrail, searched by its id, shows that it created a user `support2` with an access key of its own. What comes before the rotation?

choices.text: Nothing: `support2` stops working when dani's key does
choices.why: `support2` has its own key, and switching dani's off does nothing to it.

choices.text: Attach `AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV3` to dani, and wait
choices.why: The quarantine is a brake on dani's user, not on the user the intruder made.

choices.text: Undo what the key made: `support2` and its key
choices.why: Right. A careful intruder makes another way in before the first is closed; that door has to go too.

choices.text: Delete dani's key, so that IAM forgets what it did
choices.why: Deleting first throws away what IAM knows about the key, and CloudTrail's record is what was needed.

prompt: `plan.py` left seven `/20` blocks spare in `10.20.0.0/16`. How many `/24` subnets could those seven blocks hold?
hint: Lesson 16. Count how many `/24`s fit in one `/20` first.

prompt: Production, `10.20.0.0/16`, needs a second IPv4 range that AWS will accept and that will never stop it joining staging or the office. Which one?

choices.why: A VPC whose primary range is in `10.0.0.0/8` cannot add one from `172.16.0.0/12`.
AWS would accept it, and it is staging's range: the two VPCs could then never be joined.
Right. Same family as the primary, and it collides with nothing in the shop's plan.
Wrong family for this VPC, and inside the office's `192.168.0.0/16` besides.

prompt: Many organisations delete the default VPC in every region of every account. What does that buy them?

choices.text: A cheaper bill, since a default VPC costs by the hour
choices.why: A VPC costs nothing to have; the saving is not money.

choices.text: Room for `172.31.0.0/16` in their own plan
choices.why: Nobody needs to delete it for that; the point is what lands there.

choices.text: Nothing created without naming a VPC lands in an open network
choices.why: Right. Its subnets are all public, and whatever somebody creates without choosing collects there.

choices.text: A higher quota of VPCs in the region
choices.why: It frees one of the five, which is not why anybody does it.

prompt: `app-a`'s `AvailableIpAddressCount` has fallen from 4,091 to 12, and the tier keeps growing. What does AWS let the shop do?

choices.text: Widen `app-a` from a `/20` to a `/19`
choices.why: A subnet's range cannot be changed after it is created.

choices.text: Create another subnet from the spare blocks and place new machines there
choices.why: Right. The spare room is for this; a subnet that runs out is replaced or joined by another.

choices.text: Reclaim the five addresses AWS keeps
choices.why: They are reserved in every subnet, whatever its size, and are never given out.

choices.text: Stretch `app-a` into `sa-east-1b`
choices.why: A subnet lives in exactly one zone.

prompt: Staging shares one NAT gateway with its Elastic IP, and 300 GB a month go through it. With the lesson's prices and 730 hours, what does that NAT cost a month, in dollars?
hint: Lesson 17. Three lines: the gateway's hours, the address's hours, the gigabytes.

prompt: Tidying up, somebody runs `replace-route-table-association` and moves `app-b` onto the `public` table by mistake. What happens to its machines?

choices.text: Nothing until the next restart of each machine
choices.why: An association takes effect for the next packet, not at boot.

choices.text: From the next packet they lose the internet: they have no public address
choices.why: Right. Their `0.0.0.0/0` now points at the internet gateway, which has nothing to translate their private addresses into.

choices.text: They become reachable from the internet
choices.why: With no public address, nobody outside has an address to reach them at.

choices.text: They lose the database, since `local` belongs to the private table
choices.why: Every table of the VPC carries the `local` route.

prompt: To double the shop's way out, a teammate wants a second internet gateway on the production VPC. What does AWS answer?

choices.text: It attaches it, and the two share the traffic
choices.why: There is no sharing to arrange: one VPC, one internet gateway.

choices.text: It attaches it in another zone, for resilience
choices.why: An internet gateway has no zone; AWS already runs it across the region.

choices.text: A refusal: one per VPC, and it has no zone to lose
choices.why: Right. The rule runs both ways, one VPC per gateway and one gateway per VPC; moto showed the first half.

choices.text: It attaches it, for an extra 0.093 an hour
choices.why: 0.093 is the NAT gateway's hour; an internet gateway has no hourly price.

prompt: Staging started with one shared NAT gateway in zone a. Put in order the steps that give zone b a way out of its own.
items: allocate an Elastic IP
create a NAT gateway in `public-b` with that address
create a route table `private-b`
add `0.0.0.0/0` to the new NAT gateway in `private-b`
associate `app-b` and `data-b` with `private-b`
trap: Associating the subnets before the table has its route would cut zone b off from the internet in the meantime.

prompt: Yesterday afternoon the application could not reach the database for twenty minutes. Which tool says what actually happened to those connections?

choices.text: VPC Flow Logs, with an `ACCEPT` or `REJECT` per attempt
choices.why: Right. They record what happened, after it happened, per network interface.

choices.text: VPC Reachability Analyzer, run today
choices.why: It reads today's configuration and sends nothing; it cannot say what yesterday's packets met.

choices.text: `describe-security-group-rules` on `db-sg`
choices.why: That prints today's rules, not what happened to a connection.

choices.text: moto, replaying the same requests
choices.why: moto filters nothing, so it would let everything through.

prompt: A tester launches a debugging machine in `public-a` and, to get it working quickly, gives it `alb-sg`. What can that machine now reach that it should not?

choices.text: Nothing: rules name addresses, and its address is new
choices.why: `app-sg`'s rule names a group, not an address.

choices.text: The database on 5432
choices.why: `db-sg` trusts `app-sg`, and the machine carries `alb-sg`.

choices.text: The application machines on 8080, as if it were the load balancer
choices.why: Right. A reference trusts whatever interface carries the group, so carrying it is the identity.

choices.text: The internet on 443, which `alb-sg` normally blocks
choices.why: `alb-sg` lets 443 in from anywhere; it was never a block on the way out.

prompt: A partner at `198.51.100.7` must reach the shop on 443, while the rest of `198.51.100.0/24` is refused and everybody else is let in. Put the public network ACL's inbound rules in the order they must be numbered, lowest first.
items: deny everything from `198.51.100.0/24`
allow TCP 443 from `0.0.0.0/0`
the `*` rule, 32767, denying what nothing matched
trap: The first match decides: put the /24 deny first and the partner is refused with everyone else in its range.

prompt: Two application machines sit in the same subnet, `app-a`. One connects to the other on 8080. Which filters judge that connection?

choices.text: The network ACL of `app-a`, in and out
choices.why: A network ACL sits at the subnet's edge, and this packet never crosses it.

choices.text: None: traffic inside a subnet is never filtered
choices.why: The security groups are on each interface, so they still judge it.

choices.text: Only the security groups of the two interfaces
choices.why: Right. A security group sits on each interface, so it sees traffic between neighbours that no edge ever sees.

choices.text: Both the network ACL and the security groups
choices.why: Both apply to a packet that crosses into the subnet; this one stays inside it.

prompt: An interface endpoint for the container registry sits in the three app subnets, and 600 GB a month go through it. At the prices of 17 September 2026 and 730 hours, what does it cost a month, in dollars?
hint: Lesson 19. An hour per zone, and the gigabytes.

prompt: The NAT gateways stay for the payment provider. The application's STS calls add up to about 10 GB a month. On money alone, is an STS interface endpoint in three zones worth it?

choices.text: Yes: every gigabyte saves 0.083 against NAT
choices.why: It does, and 10 GB save 0.83 a month against 45.99 of hours.

choices.text: No: it pays for itself only above about 554 GB a month
choices.why: Right. STS calls are small; the endpoint suits traffic such as a registry pulling images all day.

choices.text: Yes: interface endpoints are free, like gateway endpoints
choices.why: Only gateway endpoints are free; an interface endpoint is billed by the hour per zone.

choices.text: No: STS cannot be reached through an endpoint
choices.why: It can, as an interface endpoint; the lesson created one.

prompt: A bucket policy can refuse whatever did not arrive through the shop's endpoint with a condition on `aws:___`, which AWS sets on every request that came through one.
Staging reads production's stock API through PrivateLink. Who pays for what, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Staging pays for its interface endpoint, by the hour and the gigabyte
choices.why: Right: the consumer pays 0.021 an hour per zone and 0.01 a gigabyte.

choices.text: Production pays for the Network Load Balancer in front of the API
choices.why: Right: the provider pays for its load balancer, which lesson 22 prices.

choices.text: Staging pays NAT processing for every request
choices.why: Nothing goes through a NAT gateway; the endpoint is inside staging's subnet.

choices.text: Production pays data transfer to the internet for the answers
choices.why: Nothing goes to the internet either way.

prompt: Production, staging and a tools VPC attach to one Transit Gateway, and it processes 1,000 GB in a month. With the lesson's prices and 730 hours, what does the hub cost that month, in dollars?
hint: Lesson 20. Per attachment per hour, and per gigabyte processed.

prompt: After an incident, 300 GB are restored from the disaster-recovery copy in Virginia to production in São Paulo, over the cross-region peering. At lesson 1's prices, what does the transfer cost?

choices.text: 41.40 dollars, at 0.138 a gigabyte
choices.why: 0.138 is the price of leaving São Paulo; these bytes leave Virginia.

choices.text: 6.00 dollars, at 0.02 a gigabyte
choices.why: Right. Between regions the direction decides, and leaving Virginia for São Paulo is the cheap one.

choices.text: Nothing, since peering has no charge
choices.why: Peering has no hourly line; the bytes between regions are still priced.

choices.text: 6.00 dollars, plus 0.02 a gigabyte processed
choices.why: Processing is a Transit Gateway charge; a peering processes nothing.

prompt: Production's VPC is in `shop-prod` and staging's in `shop-staging`, two accounts. How does a peering between them come to be?

choices.text: The management account creates it for both
choices.why: The owners of the two VPCs make it; the management account is not a party.

choices.text: One side creates it, and it is active at once
choices.why: It waits in `pending-acceptance` until the other side agrees.

choices.text: Through a share in AWS Resource Access Manager
choices.why: RAM is how the lesson shared the Transit Gateway, not a peering.

choices.text: One side requests it with `--peer-owner-id`; the other accepts with its own credentials
choices.why: Right. A peering is requested by one owner and accepted by the other, so each VPC's owner agrees.

prompt: `db-sg` in production should let in the Virginia copy's application group over the cross-region peering. Can its rule name that group as its source?

choices.text: Yes: any peered VPC's groups can be named
choices.why: Only a peered VPC of the same region; Virginia is another.

choices.text: No: that works only within one region
choices.why: Right. Staging's groups could be named from production; Virginia's range has to be written as addresses.

choices.text: Yes, once the peering is moved to a Transit Gateway
choices.why: A Transit Gateway is regional too, and the lesson gives it no such power.

choices.text: No: security groups do not apply over a peering
choices.why: They apply on both sides of a peering, like anywhere else.

prompt: A terminal has `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=sa-east-1` and `AWS_REGION=us-east-1` both exported, and no `--region` is typed. Which region does a command ask?

choices.text: `sa-east-1`, since it was exported first
choices.why: The order of the exports plays no part; the variables have a fixed precedence.

choices.text: `us-east-1`: the shorter variable wins
choices.why: Right. `aws configure list` names both in its `LOCATION` column, `AWS_REGION` first.

choices.text: The profile's region, since two variables cancel each other
choices.why: Nothing cancels; the environment still beats the file.

choices.text: Neither: the command line refuses the conflict
choices.why: It picks one without complaint, which is why `aws configure list` is worth running.

prompt: A script saved the `NextToken` from `aws iam list-policies --scope AWS --max-items 50` and passes it as `--starting-token` to `aws iam list-policies --scope Local --max-items 50`. What does the lesson say about that?

choices.text: It works: the token is IAM's marker, good for any listing
choices.why: The token is the command line's own, built around the service's marker.

choices.text: It is only good for the same command with the same options
choices.why: Right. A different scope is a different listing, and the token does not carry over to it.

choices.text: It works, if `--page-size` is the same in both
choices.why: Page size changes how many items each request asks for, not which listing a token belongs to.

choices.text: It works with `--no-paginate` added
choices.why: `--no-paginate` turns the following off and prints only the first page.

prompt: A role profile names a role whose trust policy demands a second factor. For the command line to ask for a code before assuming it, the profile also sets `___`.
Somebody captures one of the shop's signed `GetCallerIdentity` requests and sends it again, unchanged, a week later. What does AWS do with it?

choices.text: Answers it: the signature is still correct
choices.why: It is correct for its time, and the time is part of what was signed.

choices.text: Refuses it: its `X-Amz-Date` is too far from AWS's clock
choices.why: Right. The time is signed, so a captured request cannot be replayed for ever.

choices.text: Answers it, but only from the same network
choices.why: The address is not part of the signature; the time is.

choices.text: Refuses it, because the secret was in the request
choices.why: The secret is never in the request; only a signature made with it.

prompt: An SDK in `standard` mode calls an API that keeps answering `ThrottlingException`. Put what it does in order, from the first request.
items: send the request marked `attempt=1`
wait a short, random delay
send it again, marked `attempt=2; max=3`
wait a longer, random delay
send the third and last attempt
give up, saying it reached two retries
trap: The wait grows between attempts, and a random part keeps clients that failed together from retrying together.

prompt: A tool written by hand sends DynamoDB a `POST /` with `Action=PutItem&Version=...` as a form body, correctly signed. What happens?

choices.text: It works, as the same request does for STS
choices.why: STS speaks query; DynamoDB does not.

choices.text: Refused: that service speaks JSON, naming the action in a header
choices.why: Right. DynamoDB names the action in `X-Amz-Target`; a request built in the wrong protocol is refused, however well it is signed.

choices.text: It is refused for its signature, which covers only query requests
choices.why: Signing is the same in all four protocols; the dialect is the problem.

choices.text: It works, if the item goes in the path, as S3 does
choices.why: That is REST-XML, S3's protocol, which is not DynamoDB's either.
